mimicry_summary: A hoverfly resembles an ant in morphology and behaviour.
The orchid flower mimics a female bee to attract pollinating males.
A harmless snake resembles a venomous coral snake.
The common cuckoo lays eggs whose appearance often matches the host clutch, reducing rejection by incubating hosts.
Females imitate the mating flashes of Photinus females to lure responding males, which are then eaten.
The bluestriped fangblenny resembles the cleaner wrasse in shape, colour and dance to approach clients and bite scales and tissue.
Co-distributed wing colour patterns are shared among unpalatable Heliconius species, spreading the cost of predator education.
A climbing vine whose leaves resemble those of the species it climbs — the mechanism and receiver response remain debated.
A rust fungus reprograms host tissue into sweet-scented pseudoflowers that attract insects which disperse spores.
A jumping spider with an ant-like body plan and gait lives among and resembles weaver ants.
The drone fly resembles the honeybee in coloration and behaviour — receiver response has been studied experimentally.
The viceroy resembles the monarch — long taught as Batesian, its interpretation is debated since both species show some unpalatability — recorded here with the dispute visible.
The spiny leaf insect resembles foliage and dried leaves — nymphs additionally curl their abdomens to imitate ants before switching to leaf resemblance.
These crab spiders resemble bird droppings in coloration and silk-mark arrangement, hiding from predators and luring dung-seeking insects.

Müllerian resemblance is mutualistic: H. erato is equally a co-mimic pointing the other way, so each species is both model and mimic and the pair is flagged for curator review under the no-global-uniqueness policy.
